context: Italian home cooking leans on a few fresh ingredients used well. La cucina povera ('poor kitchen') celebrates farmer food. Other traditions have their own signatures.

question: A chef simmers a clear broth of fish flakes and dried seaweed. He uses it as the base for soups, simmered vegetables, and dipping sauces. Which country's kitchen does this?
choices: Japanese — a thin clear broth called dashi is the base of many dishes
Spanish — paella stock from saffron and seafood is the base for rice
French — a brown sauce called espagnole is the base for many dishes
Polish — pickle brine is the base of many soups and stews in winter
answer: Japanese — a thin clear broth called dashi is the base of many dishes
context: Dashi is the foundation of Japanese cooking — kombu kelp and katsuobushi (dried fish flakes) steeped in hot water. Western stocks use bones simmered for hours. Different building blocks.

question: A French baker is by law allowed to call her loaf a 'baguette de tradition' only if she uses four ingredients and no shortcuts. What four are allowed?
choices: Flour, water, salt, and yeast — nothing else
Flour, sugar, butter, and yeast — for a buttery loaf
Flour, milk, salt, and oil — for soft white bread
Flour, water, salt, and egg — for an enriched loaf
answer: Flour, water, salt, and yeast — nothing else
context: A 1993 French decree set the 'baguette de tradition francaise' rule — only wheat flour, water, salt, and yeast (no additives, no frozen dough). The plain loaf is law-protected.

question: A Korean family salts cabbage, packs it with red pepper and garlic, and lets it sit in jars for weeks. The cabbage turns tangy and bubbly. What is this dish called?
choices: Kimchi — Korea's tangy fermented vegetable side dish
Bulgogi — Korea's thin sliced beef grilled at the table
Bibimbap — Korea's mixed rice bowl with vegetables on top
Galbi — Korea's marinated short ribs cooked over hot coals
answer: Kimchi — Korea's tangy fermented vegetable side dish
context: Kimchi is fermented vegetables — usually napa cabbage with gochugaru chili, garlic, ginger, and fish sauce. Families pass recipes down. Every region tweaks the formula.

question: A Mexican cook pours dried corn into a pot with water and a spoon of slaked lime (cal). She lets it soak overnight. Why does corn need this old treatment?
choices: It loosens the skins and unlocks nutrients so the corn can become tortilla dough
It bleaches the corn white from yellow so the tortilla looks pale at the market
It kills bugs that hid in the dried kernels during long storage on the farm
It speeds the cooking time so the corn boils in five minutes instead of hours
answer: It loosens the skins and unlocks nutrients so the corn can become tortilla dough
context: Nixtamalization (corn soaked in alkaline lime water) goes back 3,000 years. It loosens hulls, lets corn grind into masa, and unlocks niacin. Corn-only diets without it cause pellagra.

question: A cook wraps spiced ground lamb in a cone of bread baked in a clay oven. He serves it with yogurt sauce and pickled vegetables. Which region's kitchen does this?
choices: Middle Eastern — clay-oven flatbread filled with spiced meat and yogurt
Norwegian — smoked salmon wrapped in soft pancakes with sour cream
Brazilian — slow-roasted beef sliced into warm cornmeal flatbreads
Hungarian — paprika stew ladled over wide noodles with dollops of cream
answer: Middle Eastern — clay-oven flatbread filled with spiced meat and yogurt
context: Wraps of meat in clay-oven flatbread span Lebanese, Syrian, Turkish, and Persian tables. The tandoor or saj oven gives the bread its blistered skin. Yogurt sauce cools the spice.

question: An Ethiopian cook pours a thin batter onto a hot griddle and lets it cook until full of tiny bubbles. The flat, spongy result is laid down as both plate and utensil. What is it?
choices: Injera — a spongy fermented flatbread used as both plate and bread
Naan — a soft white flatbread baked on the wall of a clay oven
Roti — a thin unleavened flatbread cooked dry on a flat iron pan
Pita — a hollow round flatbread baked in a hot oven that puffs up
answer: Injera — a spongy fermented flatbread used as both plate and bread
context: Injera is made from teff flour fermented for days. The sour spongy round is laid flat; stews are spooned on top; diners tear pieces of injera to scoop. The bread is the plate.

question: A cook stir-fries garlic, ginger, and scallions in a deep round pan over a roaring fire. He tosses in soy sauce and rice wine. The pan smokes; the food picks up a charred edge. Which cuisine?
choices: Chinese — quick stir-fry over fierce heat in a round-bottomed wok
Italian — slow saute of garlic in olive oil to flavor a pasta sauce gently
French — steady reduction of butter and stock for a sauce in a saucepan
Indian — long simmer of spice paste in a wide karahi for curry making
answer: Chinese — quick stir-fry over fierce heat in a round-bottomed wok
context: The Chinese wok-fry needs high heat and a round pan that flares the oil right onto food. Cantonese cooks call the smoky flavor 'wok hei' — 'breath of the wok.'

question: An Iranian cook makes rice the special way — letting the bottom layer stay in the pot long enough to form a crisp golden crust. Family fights break out over who gets it. What is the crust called?
choices: Tahdig — the prized golden crust at the bottom of Persian rice
Sofrito — a soft slow-cooked mix of onion, garlic, and tomato
Mirepoix — the chopped onion, celery, and carrot base of French stock
Furikake — the dry sprinkle of seaweed and sesame for Japanese rice
answer: Tahdig — the prized golden crust at the bottom of Persian rice
context: Tahdig (Persian 'bottom of the pot') is the crisp golden disk at the base of the rice pot. Cooks pat down the rice and let it brown on low heat. The crust is the prize.

question: Most Italian families eat pasta with olive oil and tomato. But the north of Italy cooks with a different fat instead, all the way through. What fat does northern Italy use?
choices: Butter — northern Italy's dairy country uses butter, not olive oil
Coconut oil — northern Italy ships in coconut to mimic southern style
Sesame oil — northern Italy borrowed sesame from medieval traders
Mustard oil — northern Italy uses pungent mustard oil from local seed
answer: Butter — northern Italy's dairy country uses butter, not olive oil
context: Italy splits at the fat line. South of Rome cooks with olive oil; north of it (Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto, Emilia-Romagna) cooks with butter and cream. Geography and climate sort it.

question: A family roasts a whole goose dark brown, slices it thin with crisp skin, and serves the meat in thin pancakes with scallions and a dark sauce. Which cuisine's signature is this?
choices: Chinese — Peking duck with thin pancakes, scallions, and hoisin sauce
German — Christmas goose with bread dumplings and red cabbage on the side
French — confit duck slow-cooked in its own fat and served over greens
British — Sunday roast goose with potatoes, peas, and brown gravy poured on
answer: Chinese — Peking duck with thin pancakes, scallions, and hoisin sauce
context: Beijing kitchens roast ducks (not goose) for crisp skin called Peking duck. The thin skin and meat are sliced and rolled in pancakes with hoisin and scallion. Centuries of imperial kitchens shaped it.

question: A French farmer ages soft cheese in caves at his farm. By law no one elsewhere can call their cheese by the same village name. What kind of system protects the name?
choices: A place-of-origin rule — only cheese from that specific village can use that name
A factory rule — only cheese from large licensed factories can use the name
A school rule — only graduates of cheese schools can call cheese by the name
A family rule — only descendants of the inventor can use the cheese name now
answer: A place-of-origin rule — only cheese from that specific village can use that name
context: France's AOC system (Appellation d'Origine Controlee, 1936) ties a name to a place. Roquefort can only be Roquefort if it comes from the right caves. Italy, Spain, and the EU built on the idea.

question: A cook ferments a paste of red chiles, sticky rice, and salted soybeans for months. It is the deep, slightly sweet, spicy paste behind countless Korean stews. What is it?
choices: Gochujang — Korea's fermented chili-soybean paste, deep and savory
Doenjang — Korea's pure soybean paste, fermented dark without chiles
Ssamjang — Korea's table dip mixed at serving, not aged for months
Cheonggukjang — Korea's quick-fermented soybean paste made in days
answer: Gochujang — Korea's fermented chili-soybean paste, deep and savory
context: Gochujang is a fundamental Korean paste — chili powder, glutinous rice, fermented soybeans, salt, all aged together. Different from doenjang (no chili) and ssamjang (table dip).

question: An Indian cook drops dough onto the wall of a deep clay oven. Minutes later he peels off a teardrop-shaped flatbread, blistered and soft. What is the oven called?
choices: A tandoor — a deep clay oven for baking flatbreads and grilling meat
A hibachi — a small charcoal grill for cooking food on metal skewers
A salamander — a top-heat broiler used in restaurants to brown crusts
A samovar — a tall heated urn used in Russia for keeping water hot
answer: A tandoor — a deep clay oven for baking flatbreads and grilling meat
context: The tandoor — a clay oven heated by wood or coals at the bottom — has been used in India and Persia for centuries. Naan sticks to its walls; tandoori chicken cooks on long skewers.

question: A cook takes a corn tortilla, fills it with slow-braised pork, tops it with chopped onion, fresh cilantro, lime, and a hot sauce of dried chiles. Which country's table food is this?
choices: Mexican — tacos al pastor or carnitas in a corn tortilla with salsa
Greek — gyros wrapped in pita with tzatziki and shaved meat on the side
Vietnamese — banh mi sandwich on a baguette with pate and pickled vegetable
Argentine — empanada hand pie of ground beef and onion fried in oil
answer: Mexican — tacos al pastor or carnitas in a corn tortilla with salsa
context: Mexican street food builds on the corn tortilla. Carnitas (slow-braised pork), tacos al pastor (spit-roasted), and dozens of regional fillings change with the place.

question: An Italian shop in Modena ages a syrup for 12, 25, even 50 years in tiny barrels of changing wood. By the end the syrup is dark and sweet enough to put on strawberries. What is it?
choices: Traditional balsamic vinegar — cooked grape juice aged for many years
Limoncello — bright lemon-peel liqueur aged in stainless tanks briefly
Olive oil — green oil from first-press olives bottled the same season
Grappa — clear strong spirit distilled from leftover wine-press skins
answer: Traditional balsamic vinegar — cooked grape juice aged for many years
context: Real aceto balsamico tradizionale (Modena, Reggio Emilia) is cooked grape must aged in a chain of barrels — oak, cherry, chestnut, mulberry — for at least 12 years. The supermarket bottle isn't this.

question: A cook breaks fresh fish into clean cuts, presses each one onto small mounds of seasoned rice, and serves with soy sauce and a dab of green paste. Which cuisine's signature?
choices: Japanese — nigiri sushi, fresh fish on vinegared rice with wasabi
Russian — herring on dark rye bread with butter and hard-boiled egg
Hawaiian — diced raw tuna with soy and sesame served in a bowl
Peruvian — raw fish dressed with lime juice, onion, and aji chili
answer: Japanese — nigiri sushi, fresh fish on vinegared rice with wasabi
context: Nigiri-zushi (Edo, early 1800s) is the fish-on-rice style we now picture. Hand-pressed rice, a slice of fresh fish, wasabi between. Sashimi (no rice) and ceviche (lime-cured) are different dishes.

question: A Texan smokes a whole beef cut for 14 hours over post oak. The crust turns black and salty; the meat inside pulls apart with a fork. Which classic American barbecue style is this?
choices: Texas brisket — beef smoked low and slow with salt and pepper rub
Memphis ribs — pork ribs rubbed dry, smoked, then sauced for serving
Carolina pulled pork — pork shoulder shredded and tossed in vinegar sauce
Kansas City ribs — pork ribs glazed in thick sweet tomato barbecue sauce
answer: Texas brisket — beef smoked low and slow with salt and pepper rub
context: Central Texas barbecue is beef — brisket, salt and pepper only ('Texas trinity' adds garlic), post oak smoke, 12-16 hours. The fat melts; collagen turns to gelatin; the crust is the 'bark.'

question: A cook in Louisiana stirs flour and oil dark in a heavy pot, then adds onion, celery, and green pepper. The smoky-dark base goes into a stew of shrimp and rice. What cuisine?
choices: Cajun — south Louisiana cooking built on dark roux and the 'trinity'
New England — slow chowder built on cream, salt pork, and clams
Floridian — fresh-fish dishes with citrus, raw tropical fruit, and lime
Pennsylvania Dutch — sweet-sour stews with apples and warm winter spice
answer: Cajun — south Louisiana cooking built on dark roux and the 'trinity'
context: Cajun cooking (Louisiana Acadians) leans on a dark roux and the 'holy trinity' (onion, celery, bell pepper — French mirepoix swapping carrot). Gumbo, jambalaya, etouffee all start there.

question: A Sicilian dish stews eggplant in vinegar with sweet raisins, capers, olives, and pine nuts. Sweet and sour at once — unusual in Italy. Which old contact brought this to Sicilian cooking?
choices: Arab traders who ruled Sicily for two centuries brought sugar and eggplant
Roman senators who held estates on the island brought sweet-sour vinegar
Norman knights from northern France brought sugar from Crusader homecomings
Greek colonists who founded Sicilian cities brought raisins and pine nuts
answer: Arab traders who ruled Sicily for two centuries brought sugar and eggplant
context: Arab rule over Sicily (827-1091) introduced sugarcane, citrus, almonds, eggplant, and the sweet-sour balance. Caponata is the lasting taste of that fusion in modern Sicilian cooking.

question: A market stall serves a noodle soup with thin rice noodles, beef broth simmered with star anise and ginger, raw beef slices that cook in the bowl, basil, lime, and chili. Which cuisine?
choices: Vietnamese — pho, a rice-noodle beef soup with herbs and lime at the table
Korean — naengmyeon, cold buckwheat noodles in a chilled clear beef broth
Filipino — pancit canton, stir-fried wheat noodles with vegetables and meat
Thai — pad see ew, wide stir-fried rice noodles in dark soy sauce with greens
answer: Vietnamese — pho, a rice-noodle beef soup with herbs and lime at the table
context: Vietnamese pho rose in the early 1900s, blending Chinese noodle tradition with French beef culture. The broth, simmered 6+ hours with charred onion and ginger, defines the bowl.

question: Most cultures eat pizza with toppings on top of the dough. But the oldest pizza tradition in Naples uses only four toppings, in a specific order. What are the three besides the cheese?
choices: Tomato, fresh basil, and good olive oil — alongside mozzarella di bufala
Pepperoni, mushroom, and bell pepper — alongside hard cow's milk cheese
Anchovy, capers, and dried oregano — alongside aged sheep's milk cheese
Prosciutto, arugula, and shaved truffle — alongside fresh white cow cheese
answer: Tomato, fresh basil, and good olive oil — alongside mozzarella di bufala
context: Pizza Margherita (Naples, 1889) has only tomato, mozzarella, basil, oil — and the red-white-green echoes the Italian flag. UNESCO listed Neapolitan pizza-making as cultural heritage in 2017.

question: A New England fisher cooks lobsters in seawater, lays them on hot stones with corn and clams, covers it all with seaweed, and steams it under the sand. What meal is this?
choices: A clambake — a New England shore tradition of steamed shellfish in seaweed
A boucherie — a Cajun whole-hog butchering and feast across south Louisiana
A fish fry — a Wisconsin Friday tradition with breaded perch and beer
A Hawaiian luau — a pit-roasted whole pig wrapped in banana leaves for hours
answer: A clambake — a New England shore tradition of steamed shellfish in seaweed
context: The New England clambake traces to Wampanoag and Narragansett practice and was adopted by colonists. Seaweed traps steam over hot stones; lobsters, clams, corn, and potatoes cook together.

question: A Japanese cook brews rice into an alcoholic drink. Unlike grape wine, rice has no sugar of its own. So a mold has to convert the rice starches first. What is the mold called?
choices: Koji — a mold that turns rice starches into sugar so yeast can ferment
Penicillium — a mold that gives blue cheese its veins and tang
Mucor — a mold used to age soybean tempeh on flat wooden trays
Brettanomyces — a yeast that gives sour beer its distinctive funky tang
answer: Koji — a mold that turns rice starches into sugar so yeast can ferment
context: Koji is Aspergillus oryzae, a mold grown on cooked rice. Its enzymes break starch into sugar that yeast can ferment. Sake, miso, and soy sauce depend on it. Japan calls it the national fungus.

question: A grandmother stuffs grape leaves with rice and herbs, simmers a chickpea-and-tahini paste smooth, and brings a platter of small dishes — olives, cheese, dips, breads. Which tradition?
choices: Lebanese — mezze, an array of small dishes shared at the start of the meal
Spanish — paella, a single one-pan rice dish cooked with seafood and chicken
German — wurstplatte, a single platter of cured sausages and pickled cabbage
Russian — borscht, a single beet-and-cabbage soup with sour cream poured on
answer: Lebanese — mezze, an array of small dishes shared at the start of the meal
context: Mezze (Arabic mazzah, 'taste') is the Lebanese, Syrian, Greek, Turkish tradition of many small dishes. Hummus, tabouleh, baba ghanouj, dolma, olives, cheeses — a meal in itself.

question: An Italian cook from Bologna would never serve a tomato-based meat sauce on long thin spaghetti. She would use a wider flat ribbon noodle made fresh with egg. What is that noodle?
choices: Tagliatelle — Bologna's wider ribbon egg pasta for ragu sauces
Macaroni — a short tube pasta for baked cheese dishes
Capellini — angel hair, a very thin string pasta for light broths
Ravioli — small filled pasta squares served in butter and sage
answer: Tagliatelle — Bologna's wider ribbon egg pasta for ragu sauces
context: Bologna's ragu (the real 'bolognese') goes on tagliatelle — a wide flat egg noodle that holds the meaty sauce. Spaghetti with meat sauce is American-Italian, not Bolognese.

question: A Sichuan cook tosses chicken cubes with chiles and tongue-numbing peppercorns at fierce heat. The dish leaves the eater with a tingling, electric numbness on the lips. Which cuisine?
choices: Sichuan — fiery and numbing 'ma la' from chiles and Sichuan peppercorns
Cantonese — gentle clear-flavored steamed dishes that highlight fresh fish
Shanghai — sweet red-cooked dishes with soy, sugar, and Shaoxing wine slow
Beijing — dough-based dishes like dumplings, noodles, and wheat pancakes thin
answer: Sichuan — fiery and numbing 'ma la' from chiles and Sichuan peppercorns
context: Sichuan cuisine prizes 'ma-la' — numb (ma) plus spicy (la) — built from Sichuan peppercorn and dried chiles. The peppercorn tingles touch receptors at ~50 cycles per second, unique among spices.

question: Most American sushi rolls (California roll, dragon roll) are not eaten in Japan. They were invented by Japanese chefs in America in the 1970s. Why was the rice put on the outside?
choices: American diners disliked the look of seaweed wrappers, so chefs hid them inside
American kitchens lacked the right knife, so chefs reversed the roll for safety
American diners disliked raw fish, so chefs needed extra rice to soak it in
American kitchens lacked rice, so chefs made the seaweed roll thicker outside
answer: American diners disliked the look of seaweed wrappers, so chefs hid them inside
context: The California roll (Los Angeles, ~1965-70, Ichiro Mashita credited) put rice outside, avocado inside. American eaters were uneasy with dark nori. Cucumber and crab replaced raw fish.

question: A New Orleans cook simmers rice with smoked sausage, ham, chicken, shrimp, peppers, and onions in one big pot. The grain absorbs the broth and turns deep red-brown. What dish?
choices: Jambalaya — a New Orleans Creole rice dish with meats and seafood in broth
Paella — a Spanish rice dish with saffron, seafood, and chicken in a wide pan
Risotto — an Italian creamy rice dish stirred in slowly added warm broth
Biryani — an Indian rice dish layered with marinated meat and slow-steamed
answer: Jambalaya — a New Orleans Creole rice dish with meats and seafood in broth
context: Jambalaya is the Creole one-pot rice of New Orleans — descended from Spanish paella but built with Cajun-Creole seasoning, sausage (often andouille), and whatever protein is on hand.

question: Most Americans think 'curry' is one dish. India has hundreds. The English word came from a misunderstanding when a colonial ate something. What did 'curry' originally mean to him?
choices: Just 'a sauce' — a south Indian Tamil word the British turned into a whole category
Just 'a spice mix' — a north Indian Hindi word the British shrunk into one powder
Just 'a hot dish' — a Bengali word the British took to mean spicy in general use
Just 'a rice meal' — a Punjabi word the British wrongly applied to any meat sauce
answer: Just 'a sauce' — a south Indian Tamil word the British turned into a whole category
context: 'Curry' comes from Tamil 'kari' — a sauce, gravy, or relish. Colonial-era English turned the broad term into a whole category. Indian kitchens cook hundreds of named dishes, each with its own name.

question: A Spanish cook sizzles slices of pork shoulder cured with paprika, then cuts thin slices of cured ham aged for two years. He pours a glass of dry sherry. Which country's cured-meat heritage?
choices: Spanish — chorizo, jamon iberico, and sherry from the Iberian peninsula
Hungarian — fresh paprika sausage and Tokay wine from the great central plain
Polish — smoked kielbasa and rye vodka from the cured pork heritage of the north
Czech — Prague ham and pilsner beer from the bohemian small-farm tradition
answer: Spanish — chorizo, jamon iberico, and sherry from the Iberian peninsula
context: Spanish cured-meat culture (jamon iberico, chorizo, lomo, salchichon) leans on acorn-fed black pigs and long mountain aging. Each region has its own specialty (Jabugo, Guijuelo, Teruel).

question: A Turkish vendor stacks lamb on a vertical spit, layer by layer, into a tall column. He turns it slowly past a hot fire. As the outside cooks, he shaves off thin slices. What is this called?
choices: Doner kebab — Turkish vertical-spit lamb shaved hot off the rotating column
Shish kebab — Turkish meat cubes threaded on a flat skewer over open coals
Adana kebab — Turkish hand-minced lamb shaped onto wide flat metal skewers
Iskender kebab — Turkish sliced lamb over flatbread with yogurt and tomato sauce
answer: Doner kebab — Turkish vertical-spit lamb shaved hot off the rotating column
context: Doner kebab ('turning meat,' Turkish) rotates lamb past a vertical fire. Greek gyros and Arab shawarma share the technique. Doner came to Germany in the 1970s and became Berlin street food.

question: Japanese soups and stews build on a thin, almost-clear broth called dashi. It is made in 15 minutes from two ingredients — no bones, no roasting. Why is this so different from Western stock?
choices: Kombu kelp and dried bonito flakes already carry glutamate (the savory taste); no long simmer needed
Fish bones at a hard rolling boil for an hour; high heat extracts flavor faster than Western stock
Dried mushrooms cooked in a pressure cooker briefly; steam draws out flavor faster than open pot
Fresh ginger and garlic blasted at very high heat in oil; the searing builds the savory base fast
answer: Kombu kelp and dried bonito flakes already carry glutamate (the savory taste); no long simmer needed
context: Dashi: kombu kelp + katsuobushi (smoked, dried, mold-cured skipjack tuna) steeped briefly in hot water. Both ingredients are pre-loaded with glutamate; the umami is already there. Western stocks build slowly from bone collagen.

question: A cook uses fish sauce, kaffir lime leaves, galangal root, lemongrass, Thai chili, and palm sugar. He balances salty, sour, hot, and sweet in every bite. Which cuisine?
choices: Thai — built on the salty-sour-hot-sweet balance with fish sauce, galangal, and lime
Filipino — built on vinegar-soy adobo and slow stews of pork and chicken in vinegar
Burmese — built on fermented tea leaves, peanut, and turmeric in hot oily dressings
Cambodian — built on prahok fermented fish paste and lemongrass curries with sour soup
answer: Thai — built on the salty-sour-hot-sweet balance with fish sauce, galangal, and lime
context: Thai cuisine builds every dish on four-way balance: salty (nam pla fish sauce), sour (lime, tamarind), hot (chili), sweet (palm sugar). David Thompson's Thai Food (2002) documents the regional kitchens.

question: Many European cuisines now lean on tomato, potato, chili, and chocolate. None of these were in European kitchens before 1500. What single 15th-16th century event added them?
choices: The Columbian Exchange after 1492 — Old and New World plants and animals traded across the Atlantic
The Crusader campaigns into the Levant in medieval times — sugar and spices arrived overland
The Mongol caravans on the Silk Road in the late medieval — eastern foods reached medieval Italy
The Viking voyages across the North Atlantic in early medieval — northern crops reached the south
answer: The Columbian Exchange after 1492 — Old and New World plants and animals traded across the Atlantic
context: Alfred Crosby coined 'Columbian Exchange' (1972) for the transfer that followed 1492. Tomato to Italy, chili to India and China, potato to Ireland, corn worldwide, chocolate to Europe — and old-world livestock the other way.

question: Italian risotto looks like a creamy porridge but never uses cream. The creaminess comes from a special starch. Which type of rice is used to make it?
choices: A short-grain Italian rice like Arborio or Carnaroli that releases starch when stirred slowly in broth
A long-grain American rice like Carolina Gold dried in the sun to develop a creamy texture in cooking
A medium-grain Spanish rice like Bomba pre-soaked overnight to release the starches before the cooking
A long-grain basmati rice from India steamed first then stirred at the table to thicken the dish naturally
answer: A short-grain Italian rice like Arborio or Carnaroli that releases starch when stirred slowly in broth
context: Risotto rice is a short-grain Italian variety high in amylopectin starch. Arborio, Carnaroli (often called the 'king of risotto rices'), and Vialone Nano all give the silky 'all'onda' (wave-like) texture when stirred with hot stock.

question: A French kitchen has five 'mother sauces.' One is built from milk thickened with cooked butter and flour. Bechamel and besciamella share the recipe — but the French use it as the start of dozens more sauces. Why?
choices: It is a neutral white base; add cheese for Mornay, onion for Soubise, cream for cream sauce, tomato for Aurore
It needs French copper pots that only French cooks own; without the right pot it burns on most home stoves
It is a sweet base; French sauces start sweet and balance with vinegar to lift flavors in the finished dish
It is a spicy base; French cooks add chili powder to the roux to give the white sauce its hidden heat
answer: It is a neutral white base; add cheese for Mornay, onion for Soubise, cream for cream sauce, tomato for Aurore
context: Bechamel = milk + roux (cooked butter + flour). Add cheese: Mornay. Onion: Soubise. Cream: Cream sauce. Tomato: Aurore. Italian besciamella stops at the bechamel stage. Carême codified the branching system early 1800s.

question: A cook chops onion, celery, and carrot fine, then cooks them slow in butter as the base for soup and stews. The mix has a French name. What is it?
choices: Mirepoix — the French diced trio of onion, carrot, and celery cooked in fat
Sofrito — the Spanish base of garlic, onion, tomato cooked slowly in olive oil
Battuto — the Italian chopped base of onion, celery, carrot, and pancetta together
Holy trinity — the Cajun base of onion, celery, and bell pepper cooked slowly
answer: Mirepoix — the French diced trio of onion, carrot, and celery cooked in fat
context: Mirepoix (named for the Duc de Mirepoix's chef, 18th c.) is onion-celery-carrot in roughly 2:1:1. Italian soffritto adds garlic and often pancetta. Cajun 'trinity' swaps green pepper for carrot. Each cuisine's foundation differs.

question: A French butcher slow-cooks duck legs in their own rendered fat at low heat for hours, then stores them sealed in the fat. They keep for months in a cool cellar. What is this technique called?
choices: Confit — slow-cooking and storing meat sealed in its own fat as preservation
Sous-vide — sealing meat in plastic and cooking it in a water bath at exact heat
Braising — slow-cooking meat partly submerged in flavored liquid in a covered pan
Smoking — exposing meat to wood smoke at low heat for hours to preserve and flavor
answer: Confit — slow-cooking and storing meat sealed in its own fat as preservation
context: Confit (French 'preserved') predates refrigeration. Duck or goose legs salt-cured, cooked in their own fat at 80-90C for hours, then stored sealed in the fat. The fat keeps oxygen out; salt and slow cooking handle the rest.

question: An Indian cook melts butter slowly in a heavy pan. The milk solids settle and brown; he pours off the clear golden fat. The clarified fat is shelf-stable for months without refrigeration. What is it called?
choices: Ghee — clarified butter with the milk solids removed, used across Indian cooking
Smen — buried fermented butter from North Africa used to season tagine dishes
Schmaltz — rendered chicken fat used in central and eastern European cooking long
Lardo — Italian cured pork back fat sliced thin over warm bread or a hot dish
answer: Ghee — clarified butter with the milk solids removed, used across Indian cooking
context: Ghee (Sanskrit ghrta) is butter simmered until water evaporates and milk solids brown and are strained off. The remaining clear butterfat keeps without refrigeration. Used across Indian, Pakistani, Bangladeshi cooking; Tibetan butter tea.

question: A street stall in Mexico City grills pork on a vertical spit, slices off thin pieces, and serves them on small corn tortillas with pineapple, cilantro, and lime. Which dish is this?
choices: Tacos al pastor — vertical-spit pork (Lebanese-influenced) on small corn tortillas
Tacos de pescado — battered fried fish in folded tortillas with cabbage and lime
Tacos de carne asada — grilled beef skirt steak chopped on warm corn tortillas
Tacos de carnitas — pork shoulder slow-cooked in its own fat shredded in tortillas
answer: Tacos al pastor — vertical-spit pork (Lebanese-influenced) on small corn tortillas
context: Tacos al pastor came from Lebanese immigrants to Mexico in the early 1900s — the vertical spit is shawarma's. Mexicans swapped lamb for pork, added pineapple and adobo (chile marinade). The fusion is now signature Mexico City street food.

question: A Chinese kitchen technique uses a hot oiled wok over very high heat. Cooks call the result 'wok hei' — the breath of the wok. What is it actually describing?
choices: A smoky flavor from oil and food briefly vaporizing and recondensing back at high heat in the seasoned pan
A loud sizzling sound the wok makes as oil hits the very high heated metal surface in the kitchen
A wisp of smoke rising visibly from the wok as it heats up that signals the right cooking temperature
A way of breathing in slowly as a cook checks the oil's smoke point before adding the ingredients
answer: A smoky flavor from oil and food briefly vaporizing and recondensing back at high heat in the seasoned pan
context: Wok hei is the unique aroma of a stir-fry done in a fiercely hot, well-seasoned wok. Oil, soy, and aromatics briefly vaporize on the metal surface and recondense on the food. Home stoves rarely reach the needed heat.

question: Most American 'Italian' restaurants serve spaghetti with meatballs, chicken parm, and fettucine Alfredo. Italians in Italy would not recognize these as Italian dishes. Why?
choices: They are Italian-American — immigrants invented them in the U.S., where meat was cheap and abundant
They are Sicilian — only the southernmost Italian region eats them; rest of Italy considers them strange
They are Roman — only Rome eats them; the rest of Italy regards them as Roman regional dishes only
They are northern — only Lombardy and Piedmont eat them; central and southern regions never adopted
answer: They are Italian-American — immigrants invented them in the U.S., where meat was cheap and abundant
context: Italian-American cuisine is its own thing. Immigrants arrived in cities where meat was cheap, so big meatballs and chicken parm appeared. 'Alfredo' is named for a Roman waiter Alfredo Di Lelio but the cream-heavy U.S. version is American.

question: A Persian cook layers basmati rice in a pot with saffron, dried lime, raisins, dill, fava beans, and chicken. He simmers and presses until the bottom forms a crisp golden disk. What is this style called?
choices: Polo — Persian layered rice with crisped bottom (tahdig), dried fruit, and herb mixes
Pilaf — Turkish toasted-rice technique where rice is browned briefly in butter then simmered
Risotto — Italian short-grain rice stirred constantly to release starch into the broth
Biryani — Indian sealed-pot rice with marinated meat and whole spices cooked dum-style
answer: Polo — Persian layered rice with crisped bottom (tahdig), dried fruit, and herb mixes
context: Polo (Persian, often translated 'pilaf' but distinct) is the layered Iranian rice with tahdig (golden crust). Dozens of versions: zereshk polo (barberry), baghali polo (dill + fava), sabzi polo (herb), shirin polo (sweet jewels).

question: A North African cook simmers lamb with preserved lemons and olives in a clay pot with a tall pointed cone-shaped lid. The cone catches steam and drips it back down. What is this pot called?
choices: A tagine — North African clay cookpot with cone-shaped lid that catches steam
A donabe — Japanese clay pot for one-pot meals cooked at the table over a small flame
A cazuela — Spanish shallow clay dish used for rice dishes and stews in the oven
A balti — Indian pressed-steel cookpot for fast curries served at the table from the pan
answer: A tagine — North African clay cookpot with cone-shaped lid that catches steam
context: Tagine names both the cone-lidded clay vessel and the dish cooked in it. The cone condenses steam back into the stew — efficient slow cooking with little water. Moroccan, Algerian, and Tunisian kitchens depend on it.

question: A grandmother makes a sour, slightly funky thin batter and ladles it onto a hot griddle. The lacy thin pancake tears off, and she fills it with a spiced potato mash and serves with coconut chutney. Which cuisine?
choices: South Indian — dosa, a fermented rice-and-lentil pancake filled with spiced potato
Ethiopian — injera, a fermented teff sponge laid flat as plate, scoop, and bread
Hungarian — palacsinta, a thin wheat pancake filled with sweetened soft cheese
French — galette, a buckwheat crepe filled with ham, egg, and melted cheese folded
answer: South Indian — dosa, a fermented rice-and-lentil pancake filled with spiced potato
context: Dosa is a South Indian classic — rice and urad dal soaked, ground, fermented overnight, then spread thin on a hot griddle. Filled (masala dosa) with spiced potato, or plain. Often eaten for breakfast with sambar and chutney.

question: A Cantonese restaurant serves dozens of small steamed dumplings, buns, and rolls from rolling carts. Diners pick what they want. This tradition has a name meaning 'touch the heart.' What is it?
choices: Dim sum — Cantonese small-plates tradition served with tea in afternoon teahouses
Banchan — Korean small side dishes served alongside the main rice and soup courses
Tapas — Spanish small plates served free with drinks in Andalusian bars and cafes
Mezze — Lebanese small starter dishes served before the main meal as openers
answer: Dim sum — Cantonese small-plates tradition served with tea in afternoon teahouses
context: Dim sum (Cantonese, 'touch the heart') is the Southern Chinese tradition of small steamed and fried dishes with tea. Yum cha ('drink tea') is the practice; dim sum the food. Originated in Cantonese teahouses on the old Silk Road.

question: A Wisconsin tradition every Friday: bars and supper clubs serve breaded perch or walleye, deep-fried, with rye bread, coleslaw, and a brandy old-fashioned. Why this specific custom on Fridays?
choices: Catholic Friday fast — meat was given up on Fridays, so fish became Friday dinner, kept after the rule eased
Federal blue laws — Wisconsin law required restaurants to serve fish once a week and Fridays were chosen
Logging-camp leftover — Friday cleaned out the week's fish stock from camp ice boxes before Saturday
German immigrant tax — early settlers paid a tax on fresh meat that exempted river fish from local rivers
answer: Catholic Friday fast — meat was given up on Fridays, so fish became Friday dinner, kept after the rule eased
context: The Wisconsin Friday fish fry rose from Catholic abstention from meat on Fridays. Big Catholic immigrant population (Germans, Irish, Polish) made fish dinner social custom. It stuck after Vatican II eased the rule.

question: A Roman-style pasta dish uses guanciale (cured pork jowl), egg yolks, pecorino cheese, and black pepper. No cream. The heat of the pasta turns the eggs into a silky sauce. What is this dish?
choices: Carbonara — Roman pasta with guanciale, egg, pecorino, and pepper, no cream
Amatriciana — Roman pasta with guanciale, tomato, and pecorino in a red sauce
Cacio e pepe — Roman pasta with only pecorino and pepper finished with pasta water
Bolognese — Bologna's slow-cooked meat sauce of beef, pork, milk, and white wine
answer: Carbonara — Roman pasta with guanciale, egg, pecorino, and pepper, no cream
context: Roman carbonara (mid-20th c., possibly involving American GIs and bacon-and-eggs) has no cream — that's the American version. Real carbonara is pasta + guanciale rendered crisp + raw egg yolks tempered + grated pecorino + cracked pepper.

question: A Lebanese cook chops parsley fine, mixes it with cracked wheat, mint, tomato, onion, olive oil, lemon. The dish is over half herbs. What is it?
choices: Tabouleh — Lebanese salad mostly of parsley with cracked wheat as accent
Fattoush — Lebanese salad of mixed greens, tomato, and crispy toasted pita
Mujadara — Lebanese lentil and rice dish topped with deeply caramelized onion
Kibbeh — Lebanese ground meat and bulgur croquette fried or eaten raw fresh
answer: Tabouleh — Lebanese salad mostly of parsley with cracked wheat as accent
context: Tabouleh (Levantine) is fundamentally an herb salad — fresh flat-leaf parsley dominates, with mint, tomato, onion, lemon, olive oil, and bulgur (cracked wheat) as accent. American 'tabouleh' over-weights the wheat.

question: A French baker's croissant uses flour, water, salt, yeast, and butter — but the structure of hundreds of paper-thin layers comes from a specific technique. What is the technique called?
choices: Lamination — folding butter into dough repeatedly to create alternating layers
Autolyse — resting flour and water before adding salt and yeast for hydration
Bassinage — slowly adding extra water to dough late in mixing for higher hydration
Retardation — chilling shaped pastries overnight in the fridge to develop flavor
answer: Lamination — folding butter into dough repeatedly to create alternating layers
context: Lamination layers cold butter inside dough, then rolls and folds (turns). Four turns of three give ~81 layers; in the oven the butter's water turns to steam, separating each layer. Croissant, pain au chocolat, puff pastry.

question: Most cultures think of pork as a single meat. The Iberian peninsula makes a distinction — only pigs that ate a specific food during their final months of life can earn the top label. What food?
choices: Acorns — Spanish ibérico pigs forage on acorns (bellota) for the highest grade ham
Truffles — Spanish ibérico pigs are fed truffles for the highest grade ham label
Chestnuts — Spanish ibérico pigs are fed chestnuts for the highest grade ham label
Olives — Spanish ibérico pigs are fed pressed olives for the highest grade label
answer: Acorns — Spanish ibérico pigs forage on acorns (bellota) for the highest grade ham
context: Spain's jamón ibérico de bellota comes from black Iberian pigs grazing on acorns (bellotas) in oak dehesa Oct-Feb. Acorn fat is high in oleic acid (same as olive oil) — earning the nickname 'olive trees on legs.'

question: A Korean grandmother sets out a long table: rice, soup, a main, and 10 small dishes — pickled radish, marinated spinach, anchovies, seasoned bean sprouts, kimchi. The little side dishes have a name. What is it?
choices: Banchan — the array of small side dishes that fill a Korean table at any meal
Bento — the Japanese boxed lunch with rice and several small compartments
Thali — the Indian round platter with rice, dal, and several small bowls of curries
Smorgasbord — the Swedish buffet of fish, cold meats, salads, and pickles on a long table
answer: Banchan — the array of small side dishes that fill a Korean table at any meal
context: Banchan (Korean) are the array of small side dishes that come with every Korean meal — anywhere from 3 to 12 or more. Kimchi is always present; the rest rotate by season. The meal architecture is rice + soup + main + banchan.

question: An Italian cured meat from Parma is salt-cured for a month, then air-aged in cellars for 18 to 24 months. The cured ham is sliced paper-thin and served raw. What is it?
choices: Prosciutto di Parma — Italian dry-cured ham aged in cool Apennine air for over a year
Bresaola della Valtellina — Italian dry-cured beef aged in alpine air for several months
Speck Alto Adige — Italian cured ham lightly smoked in the South Tyrol Alpine region
Coppa di Parma — Italian cured pork shoulder neck aged hanging in cool cellars too
answer: Prosciutto di Parma — Italian dry-cured ham aged in cool Apennine air for over a year
context: Prosciutto di Parma is salt-cured pork hind leg, air-aged 18+ months in the Apennine hills near Parma where the cool dry air shapes the flavor. PDO-protected. Sliced paper-thin and served raw with bread or melon.

question: Italian cheese is regional, not generic. Parmigiano-Reggiano can only come from a specific stretch of land between Parma, Reggio Emilia, Modena, Mantua, and Bologna. What does this strict rule protect?
choices: It links milk, local cheesemaker tradition, and the name; copies elsewhere cannot use the name 'Parmigiano'
It protects dairy farmers from outside competition by making out-of-area cheese illegal across the EU
It protects the consumer from sour milk by allowing only the freshest hand-milked cows in the area
It protects the climate; the region's air carries the right molds for the cheese to ripen correctly
answer: It links milk, local cheesemaker tradition, and the name; copies elsewhere cannot use the name 'Parmigiano'
context: Italy's DOP (Denominazione di Origine Protetta) and the EU PDO scheme tie a name to a place. Parmigiano-Reggiano is the only legal name; other hard Italian cheeses (Grana Padano) have their own DOP. American 'parmesan' isn't this cheese.

question: A Caribbean cook stews chicken in vinegar, soy sauce, garlic, bay leaves, and black pepper. The mix comes from Filipino kitchens — a sweet-sour stew that keeps without refrigeration. What is it?
choices: Adobo — Filipino vinegar-soy braise of meat that keeps days unrefrigerated
Jerk chicken — Jamaican grilled chicken in a hot allspice-and-Scotch-bonnet rub
Sancocho — Dominican stew of meat with starchy root vegetables in a thick broth
Mole poblano — Mexican slow-cooked sauce of chiles, nuts, seeds, and chocolate dark
answer: Adobo — Filipino vinegar-soy braise of meat that keeps days unrefrigerated
context: Filipino adobo (the Spanish word, but the dish is older than colonial contact) is meat braised in vinegar plus soy or salt. The vinegar acidity preserves the dish for days in tropical heat. Every Filipino family has its own version.

question: A French regional cuisine uses cream, butter, apples, and cider rather than wine — and Camembert and Pont-l'Eveque are its cheeses. Which region is this?
choices: Normandy — France's dairy, apple, and cider region in the northwest
Provence — France's olive oil, herb, and tomato region in the southeast on the coast
Alsace — France's white wine, choucroute, and pork region on the German border
Brittany — France's salt butter and buckwheat galette region on the rough Atlantic
answer: Normandy — France's dairy, apple, and cider region in the northwest
context: Normandy faces the English Channel — cool wet pasture land good for cattle. Cream and butter dominate; calvados (apple brandy) and cider replace wine. Camembert (Marie Harel, 1791), Pont-l'Évêque, and Livarot are the regional cheeses.

question: A Lyonnaise cook splits a winter morning between charcuterie shops and tiny bistros, eating small dishes and drinking Beaujolais before noon. The tradition has a name. What is it called, and what kind of food does it feature?
answer: Mâchon, Lyon's morning meal tradition for workers, centered on hearty charcuterie dishes
choices: Mâchon, Lyon's morning meal tradition for workers, centered on hearty charcuterie dishes
Brunch lyonnais, a postwar copy of the American Sunday brunch with eggs and pancakes added
Apéritif royal, Louis XIV's invention of a morning food court for the visiting French aristocracy
Petit-déjeuner standard, France's identical-everywhere morning meal originating in Lyon's bakery
context: Mâchon is a Lyon working-class tradition — a hearty mid-morning meal of charcuterie (saucisson, andouillette, sabodet), often with a glass of Beaujolais. The bouchons (small Lyonnaise restaurants) preserve the tradition. The word 'mâchon' comes from 'mâcher,' to chew.

question: A Korean restaurant table has a built-in grill. Diners cook thin marinated beef on it, wrap pieces in lettuce leaves with garlic and ssamjang dipping paste. Which dish style is this?
choices: Bulgogi — Korean marinated beef grilled at the table and wrapped in lettuce
Bibimbap — Korean mixed-rice bowl topped with vegetables, meat, egg, gochujang sauce
Japchae — Korean glass-noodle stir-fry with vegetables and beef in light soy sauce
Tteokbokki — Korean spicy rice cakes stewed in a sweet-hot gochujang chili sauce
answer: Bulgogi — Korean marinated beef grilled at the table and wrapped in lettuce
context: Bulgogi ('fire meat,' Korean) is thin-sliced beef (often ribeye) marinated in soy, sugar, garlic, sesame, pear puree, then grilled hot. Wrapped in lettuce with ssamjang (fermented bean paste dip) and garlic; rice on the side.

question: An Indian pot of rice and meat is sealed with bread dough around the lid and slow-cooked for hours with no peeking. The seal traps steam and aroma. What is this style called?
choices: Dum cooking — sealing the pot with dough and slow-cooking with trapped steam
Tava cooking — using a flat iron griddle on the stove to cook flatbreads quickly
Bhuna cooking — frying spices and meat in oil until everything browns deeply with heat
Tadka cooking — tempering spices in hot oil to bloom flavor then pouring on the dish
answer: Dum cooking — sealing the pot with dough and slow-cooking with trapped steam
context: Dum cooking ('breath,' from Persian dampokht) developed in Mughal kitchens. Meat and rice (biryani) seal in a heavy pot with dough; coals top and bottom cook gently in self-contained steam. Hyderabadi biryani is the masterpiece.

question: An Israeli cook prepares chickpea fritters fried until crisp, stuffs them in pita with tahini, salad, and pickled mango. The fritters are a Middle Eastern street food. What is it?
choices: Falafel — fried chickpea (or fava) balls stuffed in pita with tahini and salads
Sabich — fried eggplant slices stuffed in pita with hard egg, tahini, and amba sauce
Hummus — chickpea paste mashed with tahini, lemon, and garlic served as a dip
Knafeh — shredded pastry layered with sweet cheese and orange-blossom syrup hot
answer: Falafel — fried chickpea (or fava) balls stuffed in pita with tahini and salads
context: Falafel (Egyptian Coptic origin or Levantine; both claimed) is fried ground chickpea or fava bean fritters. Levantine versions use chickpeas; Egyptian (ta'amiya) uses fava. Israeli cuisine adopted it from Yemenite and Levantine immigrants.

question: A Sichuan dish uses fermented broad-bean and chili paste — the source of much Sichuan flavor depth. The paste comes from one specific town. What is the paste called?
choices: Doubanjiang — Sichuan fermented broad-bean and chili paste from Pixian county
Gochujang — Korean fermented red chili and rice paste from northern provinces
Tianmianjiang — northern Chinese sweet wheat-flour fermented paste in Beijing kitchens
Miso — Japanese fermented soybean paste from various regions of the Japanese islands
answer: Doubanjiang — Sichuan fermented broad-bean and chili paste from Pixian county
context: Doubanjiang (broad bean + chili paste, salt-fermented months to years) is Sichuan's backbone. Pixian (Pi County, Chengdu suburbs) doubanjiang is most prized. Mapo tofu, twice-cooked pork, and most Sichuan stir-fries depend on it.

question: Vietnamese cuisine reveals two big foreign influences. French baguettes show up as banh mi sandwiches. Long noodle soup shows the other influence. Where did that come from?
choices: Chinese — long-noodle soup traditions came south with Chinese traders and migrants over centuries
Korean — long-noodle soup traditions came west across the South China Sea by sea trade
Japanese — long-noodle soup traditions came south during the Pacific War's brief occupation
Indian — long-noodle soup traditions came east along ancient overland trade routes through the Himalayas
answer: Chinese — long-noodle soup traditions came south with Chinese traders and migrants over centuries
context: Vietnam sits at a crossroads. Chinese influence (over 1,000 years of rule, Han trade) brought noodles, soy sauce, stir-fry, and chopsticks. French colonial period (1887-1954) brought baguette (banh mi), pâté, and coffee. Pho fuses both.

question: Americans assume 'sake' is rice wine — like grapes fermenting into wine. Modern food science says sake is closer to beer than wine. Why?
choices: Rice cooks, a mold turns starch to sugar, then yeast ferments — multi-step grain brewing not single-step fruit
Sake brews cold then heats briefly — the temperature swing is wine-like despite rice being grain
Sake brews spontaneously in open vats — wild yeast handles start to finish, like Belgian lambic beer
Sake brews by adding rice vinegar to sweet rice — vinegar suppresses bacteria while sugars ferment
answer: Rice cooks, a mold turns starch to sugar, then yeast ferments — multi-step grain brewing not single-step fruit
context: Beer: grain → sugar → alcohol (two steps, malt enzymes). Wine: fruit → alcohol (one step). Sake: rice → sugar → alcohol via koji mold converting starch, then yeast. The multi-step grain process makes sake structurally a beer.

question: Italian pasta shapes are not interchangeable. Bologna uses a wide flat egg ribbon; Puglia uses a small ear-shape; Sicily uses a hollow twist. Each catches a regional sauce. Which trio names these correctly?
choices: Tagliatelle (Bologna) — orecchiette (Puglia) — busiate (Sicily)
Pappardelle (Bologna) — fusilli (Puglia) — strozzapreti (Sicily)
Fettuccine (Bologna) — cavatelli (Puglia) — bucatini (Sicily)
Rigatoni (Bologna) — penne (Puglia) — linguine (Sicily)
answer: Tagliatelle (Bologna) — orecchiette (Puglia) — busiate (Sicily)
context: Italian pasta is regional. Tagliatelle holds Bolognese ragu; orecchiette (Puglia, 'little ears') catches broccoli rabe; busiate (Trapani, Sicily) spirals around pesto trapanese. Each shape was engineered for one sauce.

question: Sichuan cooking pairs two ingredients to create a sensation no other cuisine replicates — a tingling, almost electric numbness on the lips, layered with chili heat. What is the technique called, and what makes the numb part?
choices: Ma-la — Sichuan peppercorn (citrus relative) carries sanshool, which activates touch receptors at ~50 Hz
Wok-hei — Sichuan peppercorn briefly chars at extreme oil heat and the burnt oil temporarily numbs lips
Five-spice — clove and star anise together suppress chili heat signals on the tongue slowly over the meal
Doubanjiang — Sichuan fermented broad-bean paste has peptides that physically bind capsaicin receptors
answer: Ma-la — Sichuan peppercorn (citrus relative) carries sanshool, which activates touch receptors at ~50 Hz
context: Ma-la (numb-spicy) is the Sichuan axis. Sichuan peppercorn (Zanthoxylum simulans, citrus family) carries sanshool — it fires touch receptors at ~50 Hz, a tactile sensation. Pair with capsaicin chili and the brain gets numb + heat.

question: A South Indian breakfast features a thin spongy pancake with a slight tang. The batter ferments overnight before cooking on a hot griddle. What ferments in the batter, and what does it bring?
choices: Rice and urad dal soaked, ground, fermented by wild yeasts and Lactobacillus — sour, leavening, digestibility
Wheat flour and water with commercial baker's yeast — leavening only; tangy flavor comes from added vinegar at end
Cornmeal and buttermilk with baking soda — a chemical leavening that bubbles fast with no microbial fermentation
Chickpea flour and water cured in the sun — heat partially cooks the batter and gives the pancake its color
answer: Rice and urad dal soaked, ground, fermented by wild yeasts and Lactobacillus — sour, leavening, digestibility
context: Dosa batter (rice + urad dal, soaked, ground, mixed, rested overnight) ferments by wild Lactobacillus and yeasts on the grains. Lactic and acetic acids give tang; CO2 leavens; phytic acid breaks down. Idli and dhokla use the same family.

question: A cuisine prizes a four-way balance in every dish: salty fish sauce, sour lime or tamarind, hot chili, and sweet palm sugar. Rice is the staple; coconut milk thickens many curries; fresh basil, mint, and cilantro finish. Which cuisine?
choices: Thai — salty-sour-hot-sweet balance built on fish sauce, lime, chili, palm sugar
Indonesian — heavy peanut, kecap manis sweet soy, and lemongrass curries
Malaysian — fusion of Malay, Chinese, and Indian regional cooking traditions
Vietnamese — light fresh herbs and rice noodles with light fish-sauce broths
answer: Thai — salty-sour-hot-sweet balance built on fish sauce, lime, chili, palm sugar
context: The salty-sour-hot-sweet four-corner balance defines Thai cuisine. Each dish — pad thai, tom yum, green curry, som tam — hits all four. David Thompson's Thai Food (2002) and Andy Ricker's Pok Pok documented the regional kitchens.

question: Vietnamese pho appears modern but came from a specific 1900s collision. French colonial influence overlaid older Chinese influence in north Vietnam. What two cooking elements does pho synthesize from these foreign sources?
choices: French beef-bone broth (Vietnamese ate little beef before) plus Chinese long-noodle and stir-fry vocabulary
French baguette and patisserie plus Chinese vegetarian temple cuisine adapted by north Vietnamese monks
French wine-braising plus Chinese steamer-basket dim sum technique under colonial French chefs in north
French butter sauce plus Chinese clay-pot rice cooking, adapted to Vietnamese palm sugar and tropical herbs
answer: French beef-bone broth (Vietnamese ate little beef before) plus Chinese long-noodle and stir-fry vocabulary
context: Vietnam: 1,000+ years of Chinese rule brought noodles, soy, stir-fry, chopsticks. French colonial period (1887-1954) brought beef culture (Vietnamese ate few cattle — they were work animals), baguette, coffee. Pho (~1900-20, Nam Định) fuses both.

question: Moroccan and Algerian spice cabinets keep a complex blend whose name translates literally as 'head of the shop' — the best spices a merchant has, mixed. What is the blend called, and what's in it?
choices: Ras el hanout — 10-30 spices: cardamom, cumin, cinnamon, mace, nutmeg, pepper, clove, ginger, rose buds
Berbere — Ethiopian blend of paprika, fenugreek, ajwain, korarima, rue with heavy chili for fiery wat stews
Baharat — Arabic blend of paprika, cumin, coriander, cardamom mostly used in Gulf and Levantine kitchens
Za'atar — Levantine blend of dried thyme, sumac, sesame, salt, eaten on bread with olive oil traditionally
answer: Ras el hanout — 10-30 spices: cardamom, cumin, cinnamon, mace, nutmeg, pepper, clove, ginger, rose buds
context: Ras el hanout (Arabic, 'head of the shop') is the Maghreb's signature blend — each spice shop's pride, sometimes 30+ ingredients including dried rose petals, lavender, grains of paradise. North African tagines depend on it.

question: Mexican mole poblano takes 30+ ingredients — multiple dried chiles, nuts, seeds, dried fruit, chocolate, charred onion and garlic, stale bread, spices. The sauce simmers for hours. What does that ingredient list achieve?
choices: Layered interlocking flavor — each ingredient contributes one note (sweet, smoky, bitter, fruity) into a whole
Preservation across long fiestas — the mix of acids, sugars, fats stabilizes against spoilage for many days
Nutritional completeness — the spice and chile mix supplies all amino acids and vitamins in a single dish
Religious symbolism — each ingredient represents a Catholic saint; the count is fixed by tradition not taste
answer: Layered interlocking flavor — each ingredient contributes one note (sweet, smoky, bitter, fruity) into a whole
context: Mole (Nahuatl molli, 'sauce') builds flavor by layering. Each chile contributes a note: ancho is sweet-raisin, pasilla earthy, mulato chocolate-y, chipotle smoky. Diana Kennedy's Cuisines of Mexico (1972) brought serious documentation.

question: Catholic monasteries in medieval Europe invented several cheeses, beers, and liqueurs. Asceticism produced these innovations. What structural reason made monastic life create so many fermented and aged foods?
choices: Long Lenten and Advent fasts banned meat; monks needed calories from dairy, fermented veg, and brewed grain
Monasteries had unlimited time and grain with no manual labor; spare hands could experiment with food
Monasteries were tax-exempt and traded freely; income from cheese and beer financed Latin scholarship
Monasteries inherited Roman culinary expertise; the cheese and beer recipes came down unbroken from Rome
answer: Long Lenten and Advent fasts banned meat; monks needed calories from dairy, fermented veg, and brewed grain
context: Monastic life involved long fasts (Lent ~40 days, Advent ~25, weekly in some orders). Meat was restricted but fish, dairy, and bread continued. Monks bred mold-ripened cheeses, brewed beer, distilled liqueurs (Chartreuse, Benedictine). Trappist beers continue.

question: A cook makes a thick smoky paste of fermented dried scallops, dried shrimp, chiles, garlic, and oil. Spooned over noodles or fried rice it transforms a plain dish. Where did this paste originate?
choices: Hong Kong — XO sauce is a 1980s Hong Kong restaurant invention, named for premium cognac as luxury signal
Sichuan — XO sauce is from Chengdu, named for Sichuan peppercorn brands marketed since the Qing dynasty
Cantonese mainland — XO sauce comes from Guangzhou wet-market vendors selling dried seafood since 1700s
Singapore — XO sauce was invented by Singaporean Hainanese cooks combining South-East-Asian dried fish
answer: Hong Kong — XO sauce is a 1980s Hong Kong restaurant invention, named for premium cognac as luxury signal
context: XO sauce was developed in Hong Kong restaurants in the 1980s. 'XO' borrows from Extra Old cognac — a luxury signal. Dried scallops (conpoy) and dried shrimp give deep umami. A premium condiment that became a regional staple.

question: Japanese ramen looks like one bowl of noodle soup. In Japan it is fiercely regional, with four major styles each defined by a different broth and tare seasoning. Which set names the four classics?
choices: Tokyo shoyu, Sapporo miso, Hakata tonkotsu (pork bone), Kitakata (shoyu with thicker wavy noodles)
Tokyo wakame, Sapporo dashi, Hakata yuzu citrus, Kitakata kombu (richer kombu seaweed in pork lard)
Tokyo curry, Sapporo gyoza, Hakata tempura, Kitakata yakisoba (cities' rivaling wheat-noodle dishes)
Tokyo cold, Sapporo hot, Hakata vegetarian, Kitakata seafood (split four ways by season and proteins)
answer: Tokyo shoyu, Sapporo miso, Hakata tonkotsu (pork bone), Kitakata (shoyu with thicker wavy noodles)
context: Ramen is a 20th-century import (Chinese-Japanese, post-1900) that rooted in regions. Tokyo shoyu (soy-tare in chicken broth), Sapporo miso (heartier, butter-corn), Hakata tonkotsu (long-boiled pork bone, milky), Kitakata (thick wavy noodles) are the big four.

question: A Persian or Iraqi cook reaches for a dried lime — a whole lime dried until it rattles, dark inside, sour and bitter. Crushed into stews, it gives a flavor no fresh lime can. What is it called, and what does drying change?
choices: Limu omani — drying concentrates citric acid and develops fermented earthy notes the fresh lime lacks
Sumac — drying the red Mediterranean berry concentrates its sour color before grinding into powder
Verjus — pressed unripe grape juice used as a souring agent in medieval Persian and European cooking
Pomegranate molasses — boiled-down pomegranate juice used as a sour sweetener in Persian stews
answer: Limu omani — drying concentrates citric acid and develops fermented earthy notes the fresh lime lacks
context: Limu omani (Persian, 'Omani lime') is a small lime boiled in saltwater, then sun-dried for weeks. Inside it turns black, sour, and earthy. Crushed into ghormeh sabzi, fesenjan, and Iraqi stews. Drying concentrates citric acid and Maillard-fermentation byproducts.

question: Italian Parmigiano-Reggiano wheels age 12-36 months on tall shelves. Inspectors tap each wheel with a small hammer. The wheel is sold or destroyed based on what they hear. What are they listening for?
choices: A clear ringing tone — cracks or hollow spots inside the wheel produce dull sounds and mark it as flawed
A sweet note in the cheese itself — wheels with too much lactose left over get marked as low grade output
An exact pitch matching a tuning fork — the standard pitch certifies the wheel is aged to the right year
A muted thud — cheese makers want soft interior cheese, so the muted ones command the highest prices
answer: A clear ringing tone — cracks or hollow spots inside the wheel produce dull sounds and mark it as flawed
context: The battitore (tapper) tests Parmigiano-Reggiano with a special hammer (martellatore). Clear tone = uniform interior; dull or hollow = cracks or voids. Flawed wheels get downgraded to grating-grade or rejected. Consortium inspectors run this at end of aging.

question: An Indian cook from Kerala prepares fish in coconut milk with curry leaves, tamarind, and black mustard seeds tempered in coconut oil. Rice and dosa accompany. Which region's cuisine is this?
choices: South Indian — coconut, mustard seed, curry leaf, tamarind, rice — Kerala-Tamil-Karnataka kitchens
Mughlai (north Indian) — clay-oven naan, dum biryani, tandoori chicken, cream gravies of Delhi-Lucknow
Bengali — mustard oil, fish, panch phoron five-spice, sweets (rasgulla, sandesh) of Calcutta-East Bengal
Punjabi — wheat-based makki di roti, sarson da saag, lassi, tandoor-baked breads with butter chicken
answer: South Indian — coconut, mustard seed, curry leaf, tamarind, rice — Kerala-Tamil-Karnataka kitchens
context: South Indian cuisine (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra) is rice-based, uses coconut and tamarind, tempers spices in coconut oil with mustard seed and curry leaf, and has far more vegetarian and fish dishes than meat. Distinct from north India (wheat, dairy, tandoor).

question: Tomatoes were unknown in Italy until 1500. Italian cuisine is now defined by tomato sauce, but for most of Italian history there was none. What event introduced the tomato to Italy, and how long did it take to catch on?
choices: Columbian Exchange after 1492 brought New World tomato to Spain then Italy; nightshade fears delayed it to 1700s
Roman expansion into North Africa late in empire brought tomato from Carthage; Italian cooks adopted in decades
Crusader returns from the Levant in late medieval brought tomato from Persian gardens to southern Italy first
Mongol caravans on the Silk Road brought tomato from Central Asia to Venice; merchants spread the seeds north
answer: Columbian Exchange after 1492 brought New World tomato to Spain then Italy; nightshade fears delayed it to 1700s
context: Tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) is American. Spanish brought seeds to Europe ~1520. Italians, like other Europeans, feared the nightshade family (Solanaceae includes deadly nightshade). Adoption took until 1700s; first Italian tomato sauce ~1690 (Antonio Latini).

question: A Cantonese chef simmers chicken, pork, ham, and dried scallop for hours to make 'superior stock.' It is the base of many fine dishes. What role does superior stock play that water or a single-bone stock cannot?
choices: Layered concentrated umami from animal protein plus dried-seafood glutamate — depth no one ingredient gives
It carries no flavor of its own but extracts flavor from the dish — a colorless flavor solvent for delicate fish
It thickens with collagen so heavily that Cantonese sauces need no starch — the broth binds into a savory gel
It supplies vitamins lost in a rice-heavy diet — providing nutrients that plain water-based stock lacks entirely
answer: Layered concentrated umami from animal protein plus dried-seafood glutamate — depth no one ingredient gives
context: Cantonese superior stock (seung tong) layers fresh chicken, pork bones, Jinhua ham, dried scallops or shrimp. Hours of slow simmer extract gelatin, free amino acids, and concentrated glutamate. The clear liquid is the canvas for delicate Cantonese dishes (shark fin, abalone, fine fish).

question: A Mexican corn tortilla and an Indian roti both look like simple flatbread — grain ground to flour, mixed with water, pressed thin, cooked on a hot surface. But corn tortilla requires a step the wheat roti does not. What step?
choices: Mexican tortilla needs nixtamalization (lime soak) to bind dough and release niacin; Indian roti binds via wheat gluten alone
Mexican tortilla ferments overnight for flavor; Indian roti also ferments but uses sourdough culture instead of lactic bacteria
Mexican tortilla needs high-heat milling to develop starch; Indian roti uses whole-wheat flour keeping its enzymes and proteins
Mexican tortilla and Indian roti use identical processing; the difference is purely grain and climate of historical development
answer: Mexican tortilla needs nixtamalization (lime soak) to bind dough and release niacin; Indian roti binds via wheat gluten alone
context: Corn (Zea mays) is missing usable niacin and the dough-binding proteins of wheat. Nixtamalization (Nahuatl nixtli + tamalli) — soaking corn in lime water — releases niacin, loosens hulls, lets corn grind into elastic masa. Without it, corn-only diets cause pellagra.

question: A Korean fermented soybean paste is darker, saltier, and more pungent than Japanese miso despite a similar concept. Made into stews (jjigae) and as the base of ssamjang. What is the paste called, and how does it differ from miso?
choices: Doenjang — Korean soybean paste fermented without rice koji, using whole bricks aged for months, fuller flavor
Gochujang — Korean fermented chili-soybean paste, sweet from glutinous rice and red from gochugaru chili
Cheonggukjang — Korean rapid-fermented soybean paste made in two-three days, sticky and very pungent
Ssamjang — Korean table-condiment mix of gochujang and doenjang with garlic and sesame oil, not aged
answer: Doenjang — Korean soybean paste fermented without rice koji, using whole bricks aged for months, fuller flavor
context: Doenjang ferments from soybean bricks (meju) hung to dry, inoculated with airborne Bacillus and molds, then aged in brine. No rice koji is used (unlike Japanese miso, which depends on koji). Result: darker, saltier, fuller. Doenjang jjigae and ssamjang are core dishes.

question: A cook in southern Italy fries thin slices of eggplant in olive oil, layers them with tomato sauce and mozzarella, and bakes the dish. The version that traveled to America became 'eggplant parm.' Where in Italy did the original come from?
choices: Campania (Naples region) — parmigiana di melanzane traces to southern Italy, claims also from Sicily-Calabria
Tuscany (Florence region) — parmigiana di melanzane is a 16th-century Florentine Medici-court invention
Emilia-Romagna (Parma region) — parmigiana di melanzane originated in Parma where Parmigiano cheese came
Piedmont (Turin region) — parmigiana di melanzane was developed in northern Italian dairies as a first course
answer: Campania (Naples region) — parmigiana di melanzane traces to southern Italy, claims also from Sicily-Calabria
context: Parmigiana di melanzane (eggplant parmigiana) claims origins in Campania (Naples), Sicily, and Calabria. The 'parmigiana' name likely refers to layered overlapping (like Parma roof tiles), not the cheese. American 'chicken parm' is a U.S. variant of the dish.

question: Indian and Persian cooking share many elements — biryani, kebab, the tandoor, saffron rice. The shared culinary inheritance is no coincidence. What historical contact produced the overlap?
choices: The Mughal Empire (1526-1857) was a Persianate Muslim dynasty in India; its court brought Persian to north India
British colonial period in both India and Persia spread English cooking that made rice dishes (pulao) in both
Greek influence after Alexander reached both regions; Hellenistic dining shaped both cuisines via Bactrian transit
Mongol caravans crossing both regions brought standard Central Asian recipes that overlay both cuisines alike
answer: The Mughal Empire (1526-1857) was a Persianate Muslim dynasty in India; its court brought Persian to north India
context: The Mughal Empire was founded by Babur (1526), a Timurid descendant of Tamerlane and Genghis Khan. The court spoke Persian and brought Persian-Turkic culinary practices: kebab, biryani, korma, rice pilaf, almond-saffron sauces, tandoor. Indo-Persian cuisine of Delhi-Lucknow is the lasting fusion.

question: An Ethiopian cook makes a fiery red spice paste — chiles, garlic, ginger, fenugreek, ajwain, korarima (Ethiopian cardamom), and 8-12 other spices — that goes into nearly every stew (wat). What is the paste called?
choices: Berbere — Ethiopian-Eritrean red spice blend with paprika, fenugreek, ajwain, korarima, chiles, base of wat
Mitmita — Ethiopian peppery powder of bird's-eye chili, cardamom, clove, salt, for raw meat (kitfo)
Awaze — Ethiopian table sauce of berbere mixed with wine or oil for dipping bread or meat fresh
Niter kibbeh — Ethiopian spiced clarified butter with garlic, ginger, fenugreek, used as cooking fat
answer: Berbere — Ethiopian-Eritrean red spice blend with paprika, fenugreek, ajwain, korarima, chiles, base of wat
context: Berbere is Ethiopia's signature spice blend. Marcus Samuelsson and Yohanis Gebreyesus document the kitchen; doro wat (chicken stew with berbere and slow-cooked onion) is the national dish. Eaten with injera (fermented teff flatbread used as plate and utensil).

question: A North Carolina barbecue place serves shredded pork shoulder with a thin tangy sauce — mostly vinegar, with red pepper flakes and salt. Almost no tomato or sugar. Which regional sauce style is this?
choices: Eastern Carolina vinegar sauce — the oldest U.S. barbecue style, from colonial whole-hog with cider vinegar
Western Carolina tomato sauce — adds tomato concentrate and brown sugar to vinegar for sweet acidic balance
South Carolina mustard sauce — yellow mustard, vinegar, sugar, from German Lutheran settler heritage
Memphis dry-rub style — paprika, garlic, brown sugar rubbed deep on meat then smoked without any sauce
answer: Eastern Carolina vinegar sauce — the oldest U.S. barbecue style, from colonial whole-hog with cider vinegar
context: American BBQ splits by region. Eastern North Carolina is whole-hog with thin vinegar-pepper sauce — the oldest style, traceable to colonial cooking. Lexington (western NC) adds tomato. South Carolina mustard sauce reflects German Lutheran settlement. Kansas City and Texas each have their own.

question: Japanese miso comes in many colors. White (shiro) is mild and slightly sweet; red (aka) is salty and pungent. The difference is not just color. What chemistry separates them?
choices: Shiro ferments briefly (weeks) high-koji; aka ferments long (months-years) higher salt; more Maillard browning
Shiro uses white soybeans, aka uses red soybeans; both ferment the same time, bean variety alone makes the color
Shiro is steamed and aka is roasted before fermentation; heat treatment alone determines the final color
Shiro and aka differ only in salt content; both ferment the same time with the same beans, salt makes the color
answer: Shiro ferments briefly (weeks) high-koji; aka ferments long (months-years) higher salt; more Maillard browning
context: Miso variation tracks ferment time, koji ratio, salt level, and bean type. Shiro miso (Kyoto, Saikyo) is high-koji, short-fermented, low-salt, sweet. Aka miso (Sendai) is long-fermented (1-3 years), low-koji, high-salt — Maillard browning during aging gives the red color.

question: A Japanese fermented seasoning ages soybeans, wheat, salt, and water for months to years with koji mold. The final liquid drips dark and salty — the staple of Japanese seasoning. What is the traditional name, distinct from industrial U.S. 'soy sauce'?
choices: Shoyu — Japanese-style soy sauce fermented from soybeans plus wheat with koji mold over many months
Tamari — Japanese soy sauce variant fermented mostly from soybeans with little or no wheat, miso byproduct
Ponzu — Japanese citrus-soy mixture of shoyu plus yuzu juice and dashi, used as a dipping sauce for fish
Mirin — Japanese sweet rice wine for cooking, made by fermenting sweet rice with shochu at ~14% alcohol
answer: Shoyu — Japanese-style soy sauce fermented from soybeans plus wheat with koji mold over many months
context: Shoyu is fermented soybeans + wheat + salt + koji (Aspergillus oryzae) over months. The wheat distinguishes it from Chinese soy. Tamari has little wheat. Kikkoman and Yamasa are old shoyu houses (1600s). U.S. mass-market 'soy sauce' is hydrolyzed acid-treated soy, not fermented.

question: A Mexican mole uses dried chiles slow-toasted, soaked, ground with stale bread, nuts, seeds, dried fruit, spices, and a touch of chocolate. The cooked sauce is so dark it looks black. Which mole region's classic is this?
choices: Oaxacan mole negro — Oaxaca's darkest mole, chiles toasted to the edge of burning for the black color
Pueblan mole poblano — the brick-red mole of Puebla, lighter color, chiles toasted gently to brown only
Veracruz mole verde — the green mole of Veracruz with fresh herbs and tomatillos, no chocolate at all
Yucatecan recado rojo — the red achiote paste of the Yucatan used in cochinita pibil, no chocolate either
answer: Oaxacan mole negro — Oaxaca's darkest mole, chiles toasted to the edge of burning for the black color
context: Oaxaca's seven moles: negro, rojo, coloradito, amarillo, verde, chichilo, manchamanteles. Mole negro is the darkest — chiles (chilhuacle negro, mulato, pasilla) toasted to the edge of burning. Distinct from Puebla's mole poblano.

question: A New Orleans cook layers ham, salami, mortadella, cheese, olive salad, and Italian bread into a sandwich pressed flat. The sandwich is a Sicilian-American invention from Italian immigrants to New Orleans. What is it?
choices: Muffuletta — New Orleans Sicilian-American sandwich invented at Central Grocery in the French Quarter ~1906
Po' boy — New Orleans submarine sandwich on French bread with fried shrimp, oysters, or roast beef gravy
Banh mi — Vietnamese-French baguette sandwich with pâté, cold cuts, pickled daikon-carrot, cilantro, chili
Torta — Mexican sandwich on telera or bolillo bread with carnitas or milanesa, beans, avocado, fillings
answer: Muffuletta — New Orleans Sicilian-American sandwich invented at Central Grocery in the French Quarter ~1906
context: Muffuletta — Central Grocery (French Quarter, New Orleans), 1906, founder Salvatore Lupo (Sicilian immigrant). Sicilian-American sandwich on round bread with olive salad and layered Italian cured meats. Distinctly Sicilian-American, not from Sicily itself.

question: Persian and Turkish kitchens use a syrup made by boiling pomegranate juice until thick, dark, and tart-sweet. It glazes meat, brightens stews, and dresses salads. What is it called?
choices: Pomegranate molasses — Persian-Turkish-Levantine reduction of pomegranate juice into tart-sweet syrup
Verjuice — pressed juice of unripe grapes used as a souring agent in Persian cooking, never sweet syrup
Sumac syrup — Middle Eastern reduction of the dried sumac berry into a tart purple syrup for marinades
Tamarind paste — South Asian pulp of tamarind soaked and pressed into a sour brown paste in chutneys
answer: Pomegranate molasses — Persian-Turkish-Levantine reduction of pomegranate juice into tart-sweet syrup
context: Pomegranate molasses (Persian rob-e anar, Turkish nar ekşisi, Arabic dibs rumman) — pomegranate juice boiled down to ~1/8 volume. Tart, sweet, dark. Used in fesenjan (Persian walnut-pomegranate chicken stew), Levantine salads, Turkish marinades.

question: A Goan cook stews pork in red wine vinegar, garlic, chiles, and cinnamon — sour, hot, and spiced. The dish reflects centuries of Portuguese rule on India's west coast. What is it called?
choices: Vindaloo — Goan adaptation of Portuguese vinha d'alhos (wine-and-garlic) with palm vinegar and dried chiles
Sorpotel — Goan pork organ stew with vinegar and chili, from Portuguese sarrabulho cooked with blood
Cafreal — Goan herb-marinated chicken from Portuguese-African origin via Mozambican galinha cafreal
Xacuti — Goan coconut-based curry of chicken or lamb with roasted spices in a heavy coconut milk curry
answer: Vindaloo — Goan adaptation of Portuguese vinha d'alhos (wine-and-garlic) with palm vinegar and dried chiles
context: Goan vindaloo descends from Portuguese carne de vinha d'alhos ('meat in wine and garlic') brought by Portuguese sailors after 1510. Goans replaced wine with palm vinegar, added dried red chili and Indian spices. The British curry-house 'vindaloo' is its descendant.

question: Vietnamese coffee is brewed with a small metal drip filter onto a thick layer of sweetened condensed milk in the cup. Why condensed milk rather than fresh milk?
choices: Tropical Vietnam had no refrigeration; sweetened condensed milk shipped shelf-stable from French canneries
Vietnamese coffee beans are too bitter for fresh dairy; only condensed milk's sugar balances dark robusta
Vietnamese tradition predates colonial contact; condensed milk goes back to indigenous Khmer dairy methods
