question: A writer argues: 'Slow Food, terroir, AOC certification, single-estate olive oil — these are bourgeois affectations. The poor cannot afford them. Defenders are gatekeeping nutrition for the wealthy.' Identify the analytical move and the legitimate steelman.
choices: Critic uses egalitarian-leveling move; steelman uses Sowell compared-to-what; quality tradition creates standards and infrastructure that diffuse to lower price tiers over time
Critic uses pure Bastiat unseen move; steelman argues seen and unseen are perfectly balanced and no action is needed since markets handle the issue automatically
Critic uses Hayek knowledge-problem move; steelman argues central planners cannot know which traditions matter and should leave them alone on libertarian grounds
Critic makes no analytical move and is simply moralizing; steelman declines to engage since no substantive claim exists to evaluate or respond to in the passage
answer: Critic uses egalitarian-leveling move; steelman uses Sowell compared-to-what; quality tradition creates standards and infrastructure that diffuse to lower price tiers over time
context: The critic makes an egalitarian-leveling move (any distinction the poor can't afford is illegitimate). The steelman uses Sowell's 'compared to what.' Quality tradition creates standards that diffuse. Mass-market olive oil is better today than decades ago because high-end terroir traditions established what 'good' means. Removing the apex doesn't raise the floor; it just destroys the apex.

question: African slave-trade food history is grim but culturally generative. Captives carried oral cooking knowledge across the Middle Passage. West African inheritance is visible in soul food, Caribbean (callaloo, jerk, ackee), Brazilian-Bahian (acaraje, vatapa, dende oil), and Cajun-Creole cuisine. What does this tell us about diaspora cuisines?
choices: Diasporic cuisines preserve craft knowledge under brutal conditions; enslaved cooks adapted West African techniques to New World ingredients into distinct regional cuisines
Diasporic cuisines are essentially invented in the New World with minimal Old-World connection; African cooking has no measurable influence on any Black diaspora cuisine
Diasporic cuisines are pure trauma response without cultural content; the African inheritance story is a 20th-century academic invention without historical support
Diasporic cuisines reflect only what enslaver-class kitchens permitted; African cooks had no agency and modern Black cuisines are essentially European imitations only
answer: Diasporic cuisines preserve craft knowledge under brutal conditions; enslaved cooks adapted West African techniques to New World ingredients into distinct regional cuisines
context: African culinary inheritance is real. West African staples (okra, black-eyed peas, peanuts, watermelon, collard greens) crossed in the Middle Passage. Enslaved cooks adapted to available ingredients. In Brazil, Yoruba religious traditions preserve specific dishes (acaraje). In the Caribbean, jerk derives from Maroon traditions. Edna Lewis, Jessica B. Harris, and Michael W. Twitty document the inheritance rigorously.

question: Three regional Italian cuisines illustrate fierce regionalism. Roman quinto quarto (offal heritage); Tuscan salt-free bread and bean soups; Sicilian Arab-influenced sweet-savory. What underlying constraint shaped each tradition?
choices: Each developed under specific constraints (Rome's slaughterhouse-worker access to offal, Tuscany's salt-tax dispute, Sicily's Arab civilizational contact) that became identity
Each reflects climate alone; Rome's continental, Tuscany's hilly, Sicily's island-Mediterranean; with no other influence on what cooking developed there at all
Each was invented in the 20th century for tourism purposes with no actual historical depth; regional Italian cooking is a marketing construct from after WWII
Each follows the same template with cosmetic variation; the regional differences are surface variation on a single unified Italian culinary tradition underneath
answer: Each developed under specific constraints (Rome's slaughterhouse-worker access to offal, Tuscany's salt-tax dispute, Sicily's Arab civilizational contact) that became identity
context: Each tradition reflects historical-economic constraint that became identity. Roman quinto quarto: slaughterhouse workers paid partly in the 'fifth quarter' (offal); Testaccio cooks made the techniques. Tuscan salt-free pane sciocco: 12th-c. salt-tax dispute; the bland bread balances strongly-flavored Tuscan companions. Sicilian sweet-savory: Arab rule (827-1091) introduced sugar, citrus, almonds, eggplant.

question: American food culture has unusual regional depth. New England, Mid-Atlantic, Southern, Midwestern, Southwestern, Pacific Northwest, and California traditions are each substantive. What does this regional depth tell us about American food identity?
choices: Immigrant settlement, indigenous heritage, and varied climate created distinct foodways in each region; no single dish unifies the country and the diversity is the cuisine
Federal food programs (USDA school lunch, food stamps) standardized American eating; regional variation is largely a marketing layer over uniform industrial food
Cookbook publishing in the 19th century (Beecher, Beeton variants) created the regional traditions retroactively; before that, American cooking was undifferentiated colonial fare
Television cooking shows from Julia Child onward invented the regional traditions for entertainment; few are older than 1960 in their current form across the country
answer: Immigrant settlement, indigenous heritage, and varied climate created distinct foodways in each region; no single dish unifies the country and the diversity is the cuisine
context: American regional cuisine is real and substantive. Settlement history, climate, indigenous heritage, and immigration patterns produced genuine regional traditions. Edna Lewis on Southern, James Beard Foundation, and modern food media document the depth. The 'no American cuisine' claim is a foreigner's misperception — there's no single unifying dish, but the regional diversity IS the cuisine.

question: Chinese cuisine has a category called 'medicinal cooking' (yaoshan) — preparations drawing on Traditional Chinese Medicine theory of hot/cold balance, organ tonification, and seasonal adjustment. The practice goes back over 2,000 years. What does its persistence tell us?
choices: Food and medicine are connected categories in Chinese culture; yaoshan persists as cultural inheritance even where modern Chinese also use Western medicine for serious illness
Yaoshan is genuine scientific medicine validated by modern research; the persistence reflects accurate medical knowledge Western science has confirmed in detail across studies
Yaoshan is pseudoscientific superstition that should be eliminated; the persistence reflects educational failure and a regrettable cultural lag in modern China today
Yaoshan was invented by the Communist government; pre-1949 Chinese cuisine had no medicinal-cooking tradition and the practice is a 20th-century state-imposed pseudoscience
answer: Food and medicine are connected categories in Chinese culture; yaoshan persists as cultural inheritance even where modern Chinese also use Western medicine for serious illness
context: Yaoshan ('medicine food') is Chinese cultural inheritance. TCM classifies foods by thermal property, flavor, and meridian-organ correspondence. Wolfberry, Chinese yam, red dates, ginseng, dang gui, astragalus are used in cooking with medical intent. The practice goes back to Huangdi Neijing. Some ingredients have demonstrated bioactive properties; others unverified. Cultural fact, not endorsement.

question: Mexican mole is a category, not one dish. Oaxaca alone has seven moles (negro, rojo, coloradito, amarillo, verde, chichilo, manchamanteles). Each uses different chiles, sweeteners, thickeners, and proteins. What does this proliferation tell us about Mexican culinary aesthetics?
choices: Mexican cuisine prizes layered complexity within a unifying structural form; seven moles are variations within a coherent grammar that lets regional identity express
Mexican cuisine is fundamentally improvisational with no structural rules; the seven moles are arbitrary combinations without underlying logic at all in their patterns
Mexican cuisine is essentially Spanish with cosmetic indigenous accents; the seven moles are minor variations of a single Spanish-imposed sauce category only
Mexican cuisine is uniform across all regions; the regional-variation story is tourism construction, and Oaxacan mole negro and Pueblan mole poblano are essentially the same dish
answer: Mexican cuisine prizes layered complexity within a unifying structural form; seven moles are variations within a coherent grammar that lets regional identity express
context: Mole (Nahuatl molli, 'sauce') reflects layered complexity within unifying structural form. Each of Oaxaca's seven moles has signature dried chiles. Each region defends its mole with civic pride. Hundreds of family recipes exist within each variant. Diana Kennedy (1972) brought serious recognition. Modern restaurants like Pujol (Enrique Olvera) elevate mole — the Mole Madre is aged like vinegar, fed daily.

question: Sushi globalized in the late 20th century — from a few Tokyo shops to a worldwide phenomenon. American innovations (California roll, spicy tuna, Philadelphia roll) added avocado and cream cheese absent from Japanese tradition. What does sushi globalization tell us about how cuisines travel?
choices: Cuisines travel through synthesis rather than pure preservation; California roll created a new sub-tradition that draws on Japanese technique while serving new audiences
Cuisines travel as pure preservation; California roll corrupted Japanese sushi and the only genuine sushi is in Japan; diaspora adaptations have no legitimate status
Cuisines travel as wholesale replacement; American sushi displaced Japanese globally and the original tradition will disappear, leaving only American adaptations everywhere
Cuisines travel without meaningful transformation; California roll is essentially identical to Japanese sushi with cosmetic differences only, no real innovation involved
answer: Cuisines travel through synthesis rather than pure preservation; California roll created a new sub-tradition that draws on Japanese technique while serving new audiences
context: Cuisines travel through synthesis. Tokyo Kaikan in Los Angeles (Ichiro Mashita, ~1965) reversed the roll (rice outside, nori inside) when American diners were uneasy with raw fish and nori. California roll became a gateway. Same pattern in Chinese-American (General Tso's), Italian-American (chicken parm), Indian-British (chicken tikka masala). The sub-tradition is real.

question: An activist argues: 'The American diet is killing Americans. Diabetes, heart disease, obesity all trace to industrial food. We need policy intervention — sugar taxes, ultra-processed food regulation, school lunch reform, advertising restrictions.' Identify the bundle of moves and the legitimate counterarguments.
choices: Activist bundles Pollan reframing, Bastiat unseen costs, and public-health policy frame; counterarguments include Sowell compared-to-what and Hayek knowledge-problem
Activist makes only Bastiat seen-unseen; only legitimate counterargument is to deny unseen costs exist, which has been empirically falsified by epidemiological research
Activist makes no analytical moves and is purely moralizing; legitimate counterarguments simply decline to engage since no analytical content exists to evaluate at all
Activist makes a Hayek knowledge-problem argument; the only legitimate counterargument is to invoke central planning, which shows the argument is internally incoherent
answer: Activist bundles Pollan reframing, Bastiat unseen costs, and public-health policy frame; counterarguments include Sowell compared-to-what and Hayek knowledge-problem
context: The activist bundles Pollan reframing ('industrial food' as not-quite-food), Bastiat unseen (chronic disease invisible at purchase), and public-health policy frame. Counterarguments: Sowell 'compared to what' (poor countries face under-nutrition; cheap calories are real gain for low-income); Hayek knowledge-problem (regulators may not know which interventions help; sugar taxes have mixed evidence).

question: Brillat-Savarin's Physiologie du Gout (1825) is considered the first sustained philosophical work on food. The aphorism 'Tell me what you eat and I will tell you what you are' is his. What does his place in French intellectual history tell us about food's status?
choices: Food was treated as serious in early 19th-century French intellectual life; Brillat-Savarin wrote alongside Enlightenment-tradition essayists on cuisine and taste
Food was trivial throughout 19th-century French intellectual life; Brillat-Savarin's book was a curiosity outside main currents with no measurable influence on thought
Food was religious topic only in 19th-century France; Brillat-Savarin's work belongs in theological rather than philosophical history, and modern reading misunderstands
Food was scientific only in 19th-century France; Brillat-Savarin's book is essentially an early nutrition text without genuine philosophical content despite literary style
answer: Food was treated as serious in early 19th-century French intellectual life; Brillat-Savarin wrote alongside Enlightenment-tradition essayists on cuisine and taste
context: Brillat-Savarin (1755-1826) was lawyer, politician, gastronome. La Physiologie du Gout (1825) treats taste, hunger, gourmandism, restaurants, sleep, dreams, the philosophy of cooking. The work belongs to the French moraliste tradition (Montaigne, La Rochefoucauld) extended to food. M.F.K. Fisher translated it into English (1949). Food has been a serious subject in Western intellectual tradition for two centuries.
